Google only saw 154 words of my tomato page

October 30, 2026•code

Odlingsguiden is a React app, but every page is prerendered to plain HTML at build time. So Google gets real HTML, not an empty div waiting for JavaScript. I thought that meant SEO was handled.

Then I looked in Search Console and saw that Google had only indexed a small part of the guide. So I started digging. Turns out prerendering doesn’t help much if what you prerender is almost empty.

Collapsed sections don’t exist

A crop page has a bunch of sections. When to sow, how to grow, companion plants and so on. They’re collapsible, and the code looked like this:

{open && <div>{children}</div>}

Makes total sense in the browser. But when the page is prerendered every section is closed. So the content is never rendered. At all.

The prerendered tomato page had 154 words. The whole profile was missing. Google saw a title and some headings and that’s it.

The fix is to always render the content and hide it instead:

<div hidden={!open}>{children}</div>

Now the tomato page has about 1,490 words in the HTML. Same page, same look.

I wanted hidden="until-found" so Cmd+F could open a closed section, but React turns it into hidden="". So that one has to wait. The heavy stuff, like the nutrition chart, still only mounts when you open the section.

Buttons are not links

Second thing. Almost all navigation in the guide was buttons calling navigate(). The crop list, the category tabs, the month navigation, companion plants. It worked perfectly for people.

But Google doesn’t click buttons. The prerendered start page had exactly one <a href> on it. One.

So every page could only be found through the sitemap, and none of them got any link value from the rest of the site.

Switched it all to React Router’s <Link>, which renders a real <a href>. No visual change, clicks work the same, and the start page went from 1 link to 74.

Every URL redirected

nginx had try_files $uri/ for the prerendered pages, which live in kålrot/index.html. So /odlingsguiden/kålrot got a 301 to /odlingsguiden/kålrot/.

The problem was that the sitemap, all internal links, og:url and the JSON-LD used the form without the slash. So literally every URL I gave Google was a redirect. Search Console listed some pages twice, with and without the slash.

And no page had a canonical tag. So a portfolio link from this very site with ?utm_source=jarnesjo.com got indexed as its own page. Nice.

The fix:

location ^~ /odlingsguiden {
    error_page 404 /odlingsguiden/404.html;
    try_files $uri $uri/index.html =404;
}

$uri/index.html serves the page directly without the directory redirect. And a canonical tag on every prerendered page, so the slash version and utm links all merge into one.

Then I made it worse

My first idea was to also redirect the slash version to the one without. Clean, one URL. I added it and deployed.

Returning visitors started getting ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS.

Their browsers had cached the old 301 from /x to /x/. Now I sent them from /x/ back to /x. Browsers cache 301s hard, so they just bounced between the two forever.

Removed it the same day. Both forms now answer 200 and the canonical tag decides which one Google should use.

Lesson for my future self: never add a redirect that goes the opposite way of an old 301.

The small stuff

A few more things I found along the way:

  • robots.txt only counts in the domain root. Mine was in /odlingsguiden/robots.txt and Google never read it. The sitemap line has to be in the main site’s robots.txt.
  • Unknown URLs answered 200 with the app, because of the SPA fallback. That’s a soft 404. Every real page is prerendered anyway, so now unknown URLs get a real 404.
  • The prerender now stops the build if a URL in the sitemap doesn’t have a prerendered page.

None of this was hard to fix. It just wasn’t visible. Everything looked fine in the browser, which is exactly the problem.

Did it help?

In mid-September Google had indexed 17 pages of the guide. On 23 October it was 204, the tomato page among them, with the version without the slash as the canonical one. Clicks from search went from one or two a day to twenty or thirty. Nothing in the content changed. It was there the whole time, Google just couldn’t see it.

The lesson

Prerendering, SSR, static export, whatever you use: it is not the finish line. It only means Google gets some HTML. Whether that HTML contains what you think it does is a separate question, and your browser can’t answer it. You are looking at the page after your JavaScript ran and after you clicked a section open. Google looks at it before.

So check it the boring way. Pick one page you care about and fetch it like a crawler would:

# words, with scripts and styles stripped out first
curl -s https://lillabosgarden.se/odlingsguiden/tomat | perl -0pe 's/<(script|style)\b.*?<\/\1>//gs; s/<[^>]*>/ /g' | wc -w
# links
curl -s https://lillabosgarden.se/odlingsguiden/tomat | grep -oE '<a [^>]*href' | wc -l

Words and links. If the numbers look like 154 and 1, that is your answer. Then open the same URL in Search Console and look at the crawled page, which is the same check with Google’s own eyes.

Five minutes. It would have saved me a month.
